title: Logger framework
scopeHtml: Scope: Levels, appenders, formatters, logger hierarchy, async appender.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a logging framework (like Log4j / SLF4J / java.util.logging): code calls logger.info(...), and the framework filters by level and writes to one or more destinations in a chosen format, without slowing the application.

Clarify: levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR)? Multiple destinations (console, file, remote)? Named loggers with inheritance (app.db inherits from app)? Custom format? Async writing? Thread-safe? File rotation? (Here: levels, hierarchy, appenders, formatter, async appender.)

Worked example. A service logs 20,000 lines/s at 200 bytes = about 4 MB/s. A synchronous file write with flush costs maybe 20 to 100 microseconds, so the request thread loses up to 2 s of every 1 s of work at that rate; an async appender makes the call cost about 1 microsecond (a queue offer) and a single writer thread does batched I/O.

Industry examples. Log4j2 (async loggers on the LMAX Disruptor ring buffer), Logback with AsyncAppender, SLF4J as a facade, Android Log and Timber (tree of loggers), Python logging (the same logger-hierarchy, handler, formatter model), Serilog.

Everyday analogy. A newsroom: reporters (code) hand notes to an editor (logger) who decides if the note is important enough (level) and sends it to the printing press, website, and archive (appenders), each in its own layout (formatter).

Common interview traps.

  • Writing straight to System.out inside business code.
  • Forgetting that logging must never throw or block the app.
  • Building the message string even when the level is disabled ("x=" + expensive() costs even if DEBUG is off).

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Level (enum): ordered DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR.
  • LogEvent: timestamp, level, logger name, message, thread. An immutable value.
  • Logger: named, has an optional level and appenders, parent in the hierarchy.
  • Appender (interface): append(LogEvent), close(). Console, File, Async.
  • Formatter (interface): event to text.

Hierarchy by name: app.db.query has parent app.db, whose parent is app, whose parent is the root logger. If a logger has no level, it uses its nearest ancestor's level.

Decision gravity. The LogEvent object and Appender interface are the one-way door: hundreds of call sites and plugins depend on them. Formatter and level rules are easy to change later.

Everyday analogy. A company org chart: if your team has no rule on a topic, you follow your department's, then the company's.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing level on every logger without inheritance (every logger must be configured).
  • Mutable LogEvent that is changed after being queued to the async appender.

| Logger                    |---------->| Logger (ancestor)  |

How to read it. AsyncAppender is itself an Appender that holds another Appender; callers cannot tell the difference (Decorator).

Common interview traps.

  • Making every class a singleton. Only the logger registry is global state.
  • Having the Logger know about files or consoles directly.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Chain of Responsibility / hierarchy: an event bubbles from a logger up to its ancestors, each with its own appenders (additivity in Log4j). Why: configure app once, specialise app.db. Alternative: flat list of loggers (no inheritance), simpler but repetitive.
  • Strategy (Formatter, Appender): output format and destination are swappable. Why: plain text locally, JSON in production for ELK/Datadog.
  • Observer-like fan-out: one event, many appenders.
  • Decorator (AsyncAppender): adds queuing to any appender. Why: async is a cross-cutting concern; the real appender stays simple. Breaks when the queue overflows (policy needed).
  • Flyweight / registry: Logger.get(name) returns the same instance per name using ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent.
  • Singleton (registry): one global registry is the standard compromise; avoid more.

Worked example (level inheritance). Root = INFO. app.db set to DEBUG. A DEBUG call on app.db.query has no own level, so it climbs to app.db (DEBUG) and is logged. A DEBUG call on app.web climbs to Root (INFO) and is dropped. That is exactly what the test asserts.

Everyday analogy. Volume knobs per room that default to the house setting until you turn one up.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing the effective level by walking the parents on every call without caching; fine here, but production frameworks cache it and invalidate on config change.
  • Logging an exception's stack trace by string concatenation; pass the throwable.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (levels, hierarchy, console/file/async appenders and a test):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

enum Level { DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR }

class LogEvent {
    final long ts; final Level level; final String logger, message, thread;
    LogEvent(long ts, Level level, String logger, String message) {
        this.ts = ts; this.level = level; this.logger = logger; this.message = message; this.thread = Thread.currentThread().getName();
    }
}

interface Formatter { String format(LogEvent e); }
class SimpleFormatter implements Formatter {
    public String format(LogEvent e) { return e.ts + " [" + e.thread + "] " + e.level + " " + e.logger + " - " + e.message; }
}

/** Destination (Observer/Strategy). Each appender has its own min level and formatter. */
interface Appender extends AutoCloseable {
    void append(LogEvent e);
    default void close() {}
}

class ConsoleAppender implements Appender {
    private final Formatter f; ConsoleAppender(Formatter f) { this.f = f; }
    public synchronized void append(LogEvent e) { System.out.println(f.format(e)); }   // keep lines unmixed
}

class FileAppender implements Appender {
    private final java.io.PrintWriter out; private final Formatter f;
    FileAppender(String path, Formatter f) throws java.io.IOException {
        this.out = new java.io.PrintWriter(new java.io.BufferedWriter(new java.io.FileWriter(path, true))); this.f = f;
    }
    public synchronized void append(LogEvent e) { out.println(f.format(e)); }
    public synchronized void close() { out.close(); }
}

/** Decorator: callers return immediately; one worker thread does the slow I/O. Bounded queue = back-pressure choice. */
class AsyncAppender implements Appender {
    private static final LogEvent POISON = new LogEvent(0, Level.DEBUG, "", "");
    private final Appender target; private final BlockingQueue<LogEvent> queue; private final Thread worker;
    final AtomicLong dropped = new AtomicLong();
    AsyncAppender(Appender target, int capacity) {
        this.target = target; this.queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(capacity);
        worker = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (LogEvent e; (e = queue.take()) != POISON; ) target.append(e); }
            catch (InterruptedException ignored) {}
        }, "log-writer");
        worker.start();
    }
    public void append(LogEvent e) { if (!queue.offer(e)) dropped.incrementAndGet(); }   // drop on overflow, never block the app
    public void close() {
        try { queue.put(POISON); worker.join(); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {}
        target.close();
    }
}

/** Named logger. Name "a.b.c" inherits level from "a.b" then "a" then root if its own level is unset. */
class Logger {
    private static final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Logger> REGISTRY = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    static final Logger ROOT = new Logger("", null);
    static { ROOT.level = Level.INFO; }
    static java.util.function.LongSupplier clock = System::currentTimeMillis;

    private final String name; private final Logger parent;
    private volatile Level level;                                   // null = inherit
    private final List<Appender> appenders = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    private Logger(String name, Logger parent) { this.name = name; this.parent = parent; }

    static Logger get(String name) {
        Logger existing = REGISTRY.get(name);
        if (existing != null) return existing;
        int dot = name.lastIndexOf('.');
        Logger parent = dot < 0 ? ROOT : get(name.substring(0, dot));   // resolve parent BEFORE touching the map
        return REGISTRY.computeIfAbsent(name, n -> new Logger(n, parent));
    }
    void setLevel(Level l) { level = l; }
    void addAppender(Appender a) { appenders.add(a); }
    Level effectiveLevel() { for (Logger l = this; l != null; l = l.parent) if (l.level != null) return l.level; return Level.INFO; }

    void log(Level l, String msg) {
        if (l.compareTo(effectiveLevel()) < 0) return;             // cheap level check first
        LogEvent e = new LogEvent(clock.getAsLong(), l, name, msg);
        for (Logger c = this; c != null; c = c.parent) for (Appender a : c.appenders) a.append(e);  // bubble up to parents
    }
    void debug(String m) { log(Level.DEBUG, m); }
    void info(String m)  { log(Level.INFO, m); }
    void warn(String m)  { log(Level.WARN, m); }
    void error(String m) { log(Level.ERROR, m); }
    void reset() { appenders.clear(); level = null; }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Logger.clock = () -> 1000L;
        List<String> sink = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
        Appender mem = e -> sink.add(e.level + ":" + e.logger + ":" + e.message);

        Logger.ROOT.addAppender(mem);
        Logger.get("app.db").setLevel(Level.DEBUG);
        Logger.get("app.db").debug("query");              // DEBUG enabled for app.db only
        Logger.get("app.web").debug("hidden");            // inherits ROOT = INFO, dropped
        Logger.get("app.web").info("hello");
        check(sink.equals(List.of("DEBUG:app.db:query", "INFO:app.web:hello")), "levels " + sink);
        new ConsoleAppender(new SimpleFormatter()).append(new LogEvent(1000, Level.WARN, "demo", "formatter works"));

        // async: 4 threads x 2500 events through the worker; nothing lost when queue is big enough
        sink.clear();
        AsyncAppender async = new AsyncAppender(mem, 20_000);
        Logger.ROOT.reset(); Logger.ROOT.setLevel(Level.INFO); Logger.ROOT.addAppender(async);
        Thread[] ts = new Thread[4];
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 2500; i++) Logger.get("app.job").info("x"); }); ts[t].start(); }
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
        async.close();                                      // flushes the queue before returning
        check(sink.size() == 10_000 && async.dropped.get() == 0, "got " + sink.size());

        // overflow: tiny queue + blocked worker drops instead of blocking the caller
        CountDownLatch gate = new CountDownLatch(1);
        AsyncAppender slow = new AsyncAppender(e -> { try { gate.await(); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {} }, 2);
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) slow.append(new LogEvent(0, Level.INFO, "s", "m"));
        check(slow.dropped.get() >= 7, "dropped " + slow.dropped.get());
        gate.countDown(); slow.close();
        System.out.println("P13 OK");
    }
}

The core in Kotlin:

enum class Level { DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR }
class LogEvent(val ts: Long, val level: Level, val logger: String, val msg: String,
               val thread: String = Thread.currentThread().name)

fun interface Appender { fun append(e: LogEvent); fun close() {} }

class Logger private constructor(val name: String, private val parent: Logger?) {
    @Volatile var level: Level? = null
    private val appenders = java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList<Appender>()

    fun addAppender(a: Appender) { appenders += a }
    fun effectiveLevel(): Level = generateSequence(this) { it.parent }.firstNotNullOfOrNull { it.level } ?: Level.INFO

    fun log(l: Level, msg: () -> String) {                 // lambda: built only if enabled
        if (l < effectiveLevel()) return
        val e = LogEvent(System.currentTimeMillis(), l, name, msg())
        generateSequence(this) { it.parent }.forEach { lg -> lg.appenders.forEach { it.append(e) } }
    }
    fun info(msg: () -> String) = log(Level.INFO, msg)

    companion object {
        val ROOT = Logger("", null).also { it.level = Level.INFO }
        private val registry = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, Logger>()
        fun get(name: String): Logger {
            registry[name]?.let { return it }
            val dot = name.lastIndexOf('.')
            val parent = if (dot < 0) ROOT else get(name.substring(0, dot)) // parent first
            return registry.computeIfAbsent(name) { Logger(it, parent) }
        }
    }
}

class AsyncAppender(private val target: Appender, capacity: Int) : Appender {
    private val q = java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<LogEvent>(capacity)
    private val poison = LogEvent(0, Level.DEBUG, "", "")
    val dropped = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong()
    private val worker = Thread {
        while (true) { val e = q.take(); if (e === poison) break; target.append(e) }
    }.apply { name = "log-writer"; start() }

    override fun append(e: LogEvent) { if (!q.offer(e)) dropped.incrementAndGet() }
    override fun close() { q.put(poison); worker.join(); target.close() }
}

Kotlin note: the msg: () -> String lambda is the idiomatic fix for "do not build the string if disabled"; in Java use Supplier<String> or SLF4J's {} placeholders.

Walk-through. Logger.get("app.job") first resolves the parent app (recursively), and only then calls computeIfAbsent. Calling get for the parent from inside the computeIfAbsent lambda would modify the same ConcurrentHashMap recursively, which can throw IllegalStateException: Recursive update or hang on some JDK versions. If two threads race, both build a parent chain but computeIfAbsent keeps one logger per name.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling the registry recursively from inside computeIfAbsent (see walk-through).
  • Blocking the app thread on queue.put when the queue is full.
  • Not flushing on shutdown: the last, most important lines (the crash) are lost. Close the appender in a shutdown hook.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints a formatted WARN line, then: P13 OK

The test asserts: DEBUG is enabled only under app.db while app.web inherits Root=INFO; the console formatter output; 4 threads x 2,500 events through the async appender arrive complete (10,000, none dropped) after close() flushes the queue; and a tiny queue with a blocked writer drops events (at least 7 of 10) instead of blocking the caller.

Common interview traps.

  • Using real time in tests (Logger.clock is injectable here).
  • Asserting on ordering across threads (not guaranteed); assert on counts.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Where threads meet:

  1. Registry: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent gives one logger per name even under races.
  2. Appender lists: CopyOnWriteArrayList: reads (every log call) are lock-free; writes (adding an appender at startup) are rare and copy the array. Right trade for read-heavy.
  3. Level: volatile so a runtime change (flip to DEBUG while debugging production) is seen by all threads without a lock.
  4. Console/File appenders: synchronized so two threads' lines do not interleave mid-line. Cost: all logging threads queue on one lock.
  5. Async appender: many producers, one consumer through an ArrayBlockingQueue. Producers only contend on the queue's short lock. The consumer does all I/O.

Overflow policy (a real decision). Queue full means the disk is slower than the app. Options: block the caller (no loss, but logging can freeze the app), drop the new event (shown; app stays fast, you lose lines and count them), drop oldest, or discard only DEBUG/INFO and block on ERROR. Log4j2 AsyncAppender has blocking and discardingThreshold.

Performance numbers (order of magnitude). Synchronous file logging with a lock: hundreds of thousands of lines/s. Log4j2 async loggers on the LMAX Disruptor are reported to reach millions of messages per second because they avoid lock contention and allocation (confirm the figures in the Log4j docs for your version).

Shutdown and crashes. Async buffers are lost if the process is killed. Flush in a shutdown hook (Runtime.addShutdownHook) and accept that kill -9 can lose the tail; for audit logs, write synchronously.

Incident pattern. The disk fills up or a network log shipper stalls. Symptom: request latency rises across all endpoints, thread dump shows many threads BLOCKED in append or waiting on queue.put. Fix: bounded queue with a drop policy, a separate disk for logs, size-based rotation.

Decision gravity. Choosing "drop vs block" is a business choice: dropping debug noise is fine; dropping audit records is not. Make it configurable per appender (reversible), and keep audit logging on its own synchronous path.

Everyday analogy. A mailbox slot with a clerk emptying it: if the mailbox is full, you either wait in the queue (block) or walk away with your letter (drop).

Common interview traps.

  • A single global synchronized on the Logger class.
  • Using ConcurrentLinkedQueue unbounded; a slow disk grows memory until OOM.
  • Reading mutable fields (thread name, formatted time) lazily in the worker; capture them at call time (the LogEvent constructor does).

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• File rotation: by size (100 MB) or daily; keep 7 files; compress old ones.
  • Structured logging: JSON with key/value fields and a correlation/trace id (MDC) so one request can be traced across services.
  • Sampling: log 1 in 100 of noisy events.
  • Remote appenders: ship to Kafka/ELK/Datadog with batching and retry (reuse the retry design from P8).
  • Runtime reconfiguration: change levels via an admin endpoint or config reload.
  • Lazy messages and parameterised logging: log.debug("user {} did {}", u, a).
  • Exceptions: include stack traces; cap their size.
  • PII scrubbing: mask emails and card numbers in a formatter.

Common interview traps.

  • Logging secrets or tokens.
  • Treating logs as the only observability tool; mention metrics and traces.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Pieces: Level, immutable LogEvent, named Logger with parent inheritance, Appender (destination), Formatter (layout).
  • Level check first and cheaply; build messages lazily; bubble events up the hierarchy.
  • Patterns: Strategy (formatter/appender), Decorator (async), hierarchy/Chain of Responsibility, registry singleton.
  • Thread safety: concurrent registry, copy-on-write appender lists, volatile level, synchronized sinks, bounded queue with an explicit overflow policy for async.
  • Logging must never block or break the app; flush on shutdown.

questions.promptHtml: How does a logger named app.db.query decide whether a DEBUG message is logged?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you understand the named hierarchy, the core idea behind Log4j, Logback and Python logging.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Loggers form a tree by dotted name: app.db.query has parent app.db, then app, then the root. If a logger has no level of its own, it uses the nearest ancestor's level. So with root = INFO and app.db = DEBUG, a DEBUG call on app.db.query climbs to app.db and is logged; a DEBUG call on app.web climbs to root (INFO) and is dropped. The level check is the very first thing, before building the event.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• level is nullable; null means inherit. effectiveLevel() walks parents until it finds one.
  • After passing the level check, the event bubbles up: each ancestor's appenders also receive it (additivity).
  • Production frameworks cache effective levels and invalidate on config change; walking the chain is fine for a demo.
Root(INFO) -> app(null) -> app.db(DEBUG) -> app.db.query(null)
debug on app.db.query -> effective DEBUG -> logged
debug on app.web      -> effective INFO  -> dropped

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Level effectiveLevel() {
    for (Logger l = this; l != null; l = l.parent) if (l.level != null) return l.level;
    return Level.INFO;
}
fun effectiveLevel(): Level =
    generateSequence(this) { it.parent }.firstNotNullOfOrNull { it.level } ?: Level.INFO

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A level on every logger with no inheritance, so each must be configured.
  • Building an expensive message string before the level check.
  • Forgetting that appenders on ancestors also receive the event (double printing).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a nullable level rather than a default? -> Null distinguishes "inherit" from "explicitly INFO".
  2. How do you turn on DEBUG for one package at runtime? -> setLevel on that logger; the field is volatile so all threads see it.
  3. What is additivity? -> Events also go to parent appenders; Log4j lets you switch it off per logger.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "levels filter messages". Senior: explains inheritance, additivity, caching of effective level and its invalidation, and runtime reconfiguration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An engineer set root to DEBUG during an incident and forgot; log volume tripled and disk filled a day later.

questions.contextHtml:
A service logs at INFO in production. A profiler shows 18% of CPU in String.valueOf, StringBuilder.append and buildReport(), called from lines like the one below, even though no DEBUG output ever appears.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
logger.debug("order " + order.id() + " report=" + buildReport(order));
try { process(order); }
catch (Exception e) { logger.error("failed: " + e.getMessage()); }
logger.debug("order ${order.id} report=${buildReport(order)}")
try { process(order) }
catch (e: Exception) { logger.error("failed: ${e.message}") }
questions.promptHtml: Why is DEBUG costing CPU while disabled, what else is wrong in the snippet, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the log level to ERROR" or "Remove the logs".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How hot is this path (calls per second)? Is buildReport expensive? Do we need stack traces for errors?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap the hot-path DEBUG call in if (logger.isDebugEnabled()) until the API is fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Java evaluates arguments before the call: the string and buildReport run even though the level check inside debug drops the message. (b) e.getMessage() only: the stack trace is lost, hiding the root cause. (c) Boxing/allocations add GC pressure.
  4. How I'd verify: async-profiler CPU flame graph showing buildReport under a method that does nothing; allocation profile.
  5. Root cause: Eager message construction.
  6. Fix: Lazy messages: a Supplier<String> overload, or SLF4J-style placeholders (debug("order {}", id)), where formatting happens only after the level passes. Kotlin: msg: () -> String. Pass the throwable to error(msg, e) so the stack trace is included.
  7. Prevention: Lint/static-analysis rule against string concatenation in log calls, and a micro-benchmark in the logging library's tests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lambdas allocate a small object per call unless the JIT elides it; still far cheaper than building the report. I would not remove the logs, only make them lazy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Placeholder args still compute buildReport() eagerly? -> Yes, passing a method call as an argument evaluates it; use a supplier or guard.
  • Stack traces for every error are too big? -> Cap size or log the top frames plus a cause id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite perf incident where disabling DEBUG changed nothing for latency until someone noticed the messages were still being built.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lowers the level.
  • Hire: explains eager evaluation, uses placeholders or suppliers, passes the throwable.
  • Strong hire: points out the argument-evaluation pitfall, guards and lint rules.

questions.contextHtml:
A new Logger.get was refactored to be "more concise". Under load tests, calls to Logger.get("a.b.c") from many threads sometimes throw or hang at startup.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
static Logger get(String name) {
    return REGISTRY.computeIfAbsent(name, n -> {
        int dot = n.lastIndexOf('.');
        Logger parent = dot < 0 ? ROOT : get(n.substring(0, dot));   // recursive call inside the lambda
        return new Logger(n, parent);
    });
}
fun get(name: String): Logger = registry.computeIfAbsent(name) { n ->
    val dot = n.lastIndexOf('.')
    val parent = if (dot < 0) ROOT else get(n.substring(0, dot))   // recursive call inside the lambda
    Logger(n, parent)
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, why does it show up only under concurrency or on some JDKs, and what is the safe version?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe so it is fine."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which JDK version? Is the failure an exception or a hang? Is there another place where the map is modified inside a lambda?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert to the previous version that resolved the parent first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Recursive update of the same ConcurrentHashMap inside computeIfAbsent: documented as forbidden; may throw IllegalStateException: Recursive update or deadlock, depending on bins and JDK. (b) Two threads building chains concurrently: not a bug by itself. (c) The ROOT static init order: red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Stack trace with ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent appearing twice; a stress test with 16 threads fetching deep unique names.
  5. Root cause: Mutating the map from inside its own atomic compute function.
  6. Fix: Resolve the parent before touching the map, then call computeIfAbsent with a non-recursive lambda:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
static Logger get(String name) {
    Logger existing = REGISTRY.get(name);
    if (existing != null) return existing;
    int dot = name.lastIndexOf('.');
    Logger parent = dot < 0 ? ROOT : get(name.substring(0, dot));
    return REGISTRY.computeIfAbsent(name, n -> new Logger(n, parent));
}
fun get(name: String): Logger {
    registry[name]?.let { return it }
    val dot = name.lastIndexOf('.')
    val parent = if (dot < 0) ROOT else get(name.substring(0, dot))
    return registry.computeIfAbsent(name) { Logger(it, parent) }
}
  1. Prevention: Stress test for registry races; code-review rule: no calls that touch the same concurrent map from inside compute/merge lambdas.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Two racing threads may both build a parent chain, but computeIfAbsent keeps exactly one logger per name; I accept that tiny waste. I would not use a global synchronized on get (it serializes every logger lookup).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not putIfAbsent? -> It works but may create a throwaway Logger every time; computeIfAbsent avoids construction when present (still fine either way).
  • Loggers never get released? -> Names are bounded by source; if dynamic, use weak references.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite startup hang that reproduced one in twenty deploys because the recursive map update only blocked when two names hashed to the same bin.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says it is fine.
  • Hire: identifies recursive update and fixes ordering.
  • Strong hire: explains bin-level locking symptom, one-logger-per-name guarantee and stress test.

questions.contextHtml: Ops asks for (1) JSON output with a traceId field for ELK, (2) errors also posted to a Slack webhook, and (3) the console appender to stay human-readable locally. The logging framework has Logger, ConsoleAppender, FileAppender, AsyncAppender, SimpleFormatter. Slack calls take 300 to 800 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes are added or changed, and how do you keep the Slack call from slowing the app?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds if (json) and if (slack) branches in Logger and calls Slack inline.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which levels go to Slack (ERROR only)? Rate limit for Slack (many errors could flood)? Where does traceId come from (MDC/thread-local)? Is losing a Slack post acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; extension design, but I would not post Slack synchronously.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The design should satisfy open/closed: add classes, edit none of the existing ones except LogEvent (new field).
  4. How I'd verify: Unit tests with a memory appender; a test that a slow Slack appender wrapped in AsyncAppender does not slow logger.info (blocked writer test).
  5. Root cause / design: New: JsonFormatter implements Formatter, SlackAppender implements Appender (with a min level), reuse AsyncAppender as a Decorator around it. LogEvent gains an immutable traceId captured at creation. Logger, existing appenders and formatters are untouched.
  6. Fix (code):

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class JsonFormatter implements Formatter {
    public String format(LogEvent e) {
        return "{\"ts\":" + e.ts + ",\"level\":\"" + e.level + "\",\"logger\":\"" + e.logger
             + "\",\"traceId\":\"" + e.traceId + "\",\"msg\":\"" + escape(e.message) + "\"}";
    }
}
Appender slack = new AsyncAppender(new MinLevelAppender(Level.ERROR, new SlackAppender(url)), 1000);
Logger.get("app").addAppender(slack);
class JsonFormatter : Formatter {
    override fun format(e: LogEvent) =
        """{"ts":${e.ts},"level":"${e.level}","logger":"${e.logger}","traceId":"${e.traceId}","msg":"${escape(e.msg)}"}"""
}
val slack = AsyncAppender(MinLevelAppender(Level.ERROR, SlackAppender(url)), 1000)
Logger.get("app").addAppender(slack)
  1. Prevention: Escape strings in the JSON formatter (quotes, newlines); rate limit Slack posts (reuse the rate limiter design) and test the escaping.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not call Slack synchronously and would not give Logger knowledge of formatters. A bounded queue with a drop policy is right for Slack; for audit logs I would not drop.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Slack is down for 10 minutes? -> Queue fills and drops; count drops and keep file logs; retry with backoff in the Slack appender.
  • Per-appender level? -> Add MinLevelAppender decorator or a level field on the appender.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where an error loop posted 40,000 Slack messages in a minute until the webhook was revoked, which is why alert appenders get a rate limit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: branches inside Logger, inline HTTP call.
  • Hire: new Formatter and Appender, async wrapper, open/closed.
  • Strong hire: traceId capture at call time, escaping, rate-limited alerts, drop policy per destination.

questions.contextHtml: At 14:05 a log volume reaches 98% and its disk latency rises to 800 ms per fsync. API p99 goes from 60 ms to 11 s across all endpoints; CPU is 9%. A thread dump shows 180 of 200 request threads BLOCKED in FileAppender.append waiting on one monitor; one thread is inside PrintWriter.println. The service uses a synchronous FileAppender. Someone suggests increasing the thread pool to 400.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, mitigate, and redesign so logging cannot take the service down.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Bigger thread pool or "delete old logs" only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are audit logs mixed in this file? Can we lose debug lines under pressure? Where do logs ship (agent)? What does rotation do?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Free disk space or rotate/compress old logs, point the appender at another volume, or switch the appender to console/discard temporarily.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Synchronous appender with a global lock: one slow write blocks all threads. (b) Disk full or slow volume (given 98%). (c) GC pause: red herring, CPU is low.
  4. How I'd verify: jstack to see lock owner, iostat -x 1 for await, df -h.
  5. Root cause: Slow I/O performed on request threads under one lock.
  6. Fix: Wrap the file appender in an AsyncAppender with a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue; producers do offer (about 1 microsecond) and never block; one writer thread does batched I/O. On overflow: drop (count it), or drop DEBUG/INFO and block only on ERROR. Add size-based rotation, a separate disk, and alerts on dropped.
  7. Prevention: Disk usage alert at 80%, chaos test with a throttled disk, dashboard on queue depth.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dropping loses lines (accept for debug, not for audit; audit goes through a separate synchronous path). I would not use an unbounded ConcurrentLinkedQueue: a slow disk turns into OOM.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Queue size? -> At 20,000 lines/s, 20,000 slots is 1 second of buffer (about 4 MB at 200 B/line); size it for the longest stall you want to ride out, bounded by memory.
  • Which overflow policy for ERROR? -> Block briefly or write to a fallback; errors are the most valuable lines.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where a "full disk" paged the database team while the real symptom (all endpoints slow) was thread starvation behind a logging monitor.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases threads.
  • Hire: async bounded queue with a drop policy.
  • Strong hire: separate audit path, queue sizing math, drop metrics, disk alerting.

questions.promptHtml: Why is AsyncAppender implemented as an Appender that wraps another Appender, and how does close() avoid losing the last lines?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests Decorator vs inheritance and the shutdown correctness of producer/consumer code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Async is a cross-cutting concern: queueing should work for any destination, so AsyncAppender implements Appender and holds a target Appender. Callers cannot tell the difference. append does a non-blocking offer to a bounded queue; one worker thread takes events and calls target.append. close() puts a poison pill on the queue, joins the worker so everything queued before it is written, then closes the target.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without the decorator you would need AsyncFileAppender, AsyncConsoleAppender, and so on: a class explosion.
  • Poison pill: the worker loops on take() until it sees the sentinel; events queued earlier are drained first (FIFO).
  • Bounded queue forces an overflow decision (drop, block, drop oldest).
app threads -> offer -> [ bounded queue ] -> take -> worker -> target.append (file I/O)
close(): put(POISON) -> worker drains, exits -> join() -> target.close()

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public void append(LogEvent e) { if (!queue.offer(e)) dropped.incrementAndGet(); }
public void close() {
    try { queue.put(POISON); worker.join(); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {}
    target.close();
}
override fun append(e: LogEvent) { if (!q.offer(e)) dropped.incrementAndGet() }
override fun close() { q.put(poison); worker.join(); target.close() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Blocking the caller with put when the queue is full.
  • close() without joining: last lines lost.
  • Capturing thread name or time lazily in the worker (it would show the worker thread).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if close() is called when the queue is full? -> put on the poison blocks until space frees; the worker is draining, so it eventually succeeds.
  2. What about kill -9? -> The queue is lost; register a shutdown hook for normal exits and write audit logs synchronously.
  3. Why not use a ConcurrentLinkedQueue? -> Unbounded: a stalled disk grows memory to OOM.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "wraps another appender for async". Senior: ties it to Decorator and open/closed, explains poison-pill draining, capture-at-call-time of event fields, and the overflow policy as a business decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team lost the final stack trace before a crash because their async buffer was never flushed on shutdown.

questions.subtopic: Overflow policy for audit vs debug
questions.contextHtml: An async appender with a 10,000-slot queue drops on overflow. During a deploy the disk throttles and 1.2 million events are dropped over 4 minutes: mostly DEBUG noise, but also 38 PAYMENT_AUDIT records that compliance requires. Engineering suggests "switch to blocking put"; the SRE says blocking logs froze the app last year. The Level set is DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR.
questions.promptHtml: Choose an overflow design and justify it. What is reversible and what is not?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks drop or block globally with no distinction between log classes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is audit a legal requirement (no loss) or best effort? What is the acceptable added latency for audit writes? Can audit use a different store (database, Kafka)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reconstruct the 38 audit records from the payment database; re-route audit logging to a separate synchronous path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) One overflow policy cannot serve two requirements. (b) Queue capacity is too small for a 4-minute stall: red herring; no queue size covers an unbounded stall.
  4. How I'd verify: Counts of dropped per level; replay the stall in a test with a gate-blocked writer.
  5. Root cause: Audit records travel through best-effort logging.
  6. Fix: Two pipelines: operational logs through an async appender with a discarding threshold (drop DEBUG/INFO first, block briefly or fall back on WARN/ERROR); audit through a separate sink: synchronous write to a durable store or a transactional outbox with retry. Keep the policy configurable per appender (reversible).
  7. Prevention: Metric and alert on drops by level; a test asserting audit events are never dropped; ownership of audit in compliance docs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Blocking for ERROR can still freeze the app during a long stall; cap the block (for example 50 ms) then spill to a local fallback file. I would not make all logging synchronous to protect audit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Queue memory limit? -> Bound by count and bytes (messages can be large); cap message size.
  • Drop oldest instead of newest? -> Keeps recent events (often more useful in incidents) at the cost of lost history.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite compliance finding where "we log everything" turned out to mean "we log everything unless the disk is slow".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: block or drop globally.
  • Hire: separates audit from operational logs.
  • Strong hire: level-aware discarding, bounded block with spill, metrics, and the compliance ownership angle.

questions.contextHtml: A service logs 20,000 lines/s at 200 bytes (about 4 MB/s, 345 GB/day). Traffic is expected to grow 10x for a sale. Disk is 500 GB, retention is 7 days, and the async queue has 20,000 slots with a single writer thread. Current writer throughput on the disk is about 80 MB/s sequential.
questions.promptHtml: Will it hold at 10x? Show the numbers and what you change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more disks" with no calculation, or assumes the writer can keep up because 80 MB/s is bigger than 40 MB/s without checking disk space and queue depth.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak or average 10x? Is log content compressible (JSON usually 5 to 10x with gzip)? Can we sample? Where do logs ship?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower noise: INFO to WARN for chatty packages, sampling 1 in 100 for the loudest events.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: At 10x: 200,000 lines/s = 40 MB/s = about 3.45 TB/day; 7 days = 24 TB, far above 500 GB. Throughput: 40 MB/s is half of 80 MB/s but leaves little headroom; and a single writer doing formatting plus I/O may saturate a CPU core before the disk.
  4. How I'd verify: Benchmark the appender at 200k lines/s; watch queue depth and dropped; iostat for disk saturation.
  5. Root cause: Both retention space and single-writer throughput scale linearly with volume.
  6. Fix: Reduce at the source (levels, sampling, no per-request debug), compress on rotation (size-based rotation at 1 GB, gzip), ship to central storage (Kafka to ELK) and keep only 24 hours locally (about 3.45 TB uncompressed, so still large: sample or compress). Batch writes in the writer (flush every N ms), and parallelize formatting off the writer thread if CPU-bound.
  7. Prevention: Capacity alert on bytes per second per service, a per-service log budget, load test before the sale.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sampling loses lines (never sample audit or errors); I would not keep 7 days on the app host at this volume. Queue sizing: 20,000 slots at 200,000 lines/s is only 0.1 s of buffering, so the policy at overflow matters more than size.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Log shipper agent uses 30% CPU? -> Switch to binary or JSON with fewer fields, or send directly via an async remote appender.
  • Rotation blocks writes? -> Rotate in the writer thread by rename; compress in a separate pool.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite sale-day incident where logging volume, not traffic, filled the disk and took the checkout service down at 11 am.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no arithmetic.
  • Hire: computes volume, retention and queue buffer; reduces and ships logs.
  • Strong hire: queue-seconds reasoning, compression, sampling limits, log budget, CPU vs disk bottleneck.
